data.title: Železník – a hillfort above Dolné Orešany in the Lesser Carpathians
data.excerpt: A prominent conical hill in the valley of the Parná above Dolné Orešany, occupied from the Early Eneolithic to the 15th century and guarding a route westwards towards Sološnica and Rohožník. Its chief claim to fame is the roughly 2,000 counterfeit coins modelled on Viennese pfennigs, found on the summit and the slopes together with the remains of a forger’s workshop.

children.text: The Železník hillfort lies in the cadastral area of the village of Dolné Orešany. The best approach to it, however, leads through Horné Orešany: you need to drive through the village and then, beyond it, turn towards Lošonec and then towards Majdán, where at the spot by the Olšovský mill you leave your car in a small car park and continue along the green waymarked path past Husí stok. After roughly 25 minutes of easy walking along the asphalt road, once you have passed the aforementioned Husí stok, the fortlet of Vápenná and the line of the abandoned railway, a prominent conical hill with fairly steep slopes will appear ahead of you on the left, bearing the name Železník.

An old road, still visible today, leads up to it; it begins at right angles to the present-day asphalt road and runs from north to south, and after a few dozen metres it starts to turn right and climbs slowly and obliquely across the contours around the hill towards the summit. In the south-western part, roughly in the upper half of the slope, the road passes across an interesting small platform on which a number of medieval finds were discovered and on which the entrance gateway to the hillfort itself may have stood. This supposition of mine is not, however, as yet precisely confirmed by excavation. Not far from that spot the road then passes smoothly into a pronounced settlement terrace, originally fortified at its edges, it seems, with a timber palisade, which runs around the whole hill. The summit of Železník forms a fairly level area on which timber buildings probably stood originally. No traces of medieval stone architecture have been found so far.

The hillfort lies in the valley of the Parná, through which one of the routes westwards, specifically towards Sološnica or Rohožník, apparently ran in the past; from this its primarily strategic guard function follows almost beyond doubt. The fortification of Vápenica, several hundred metres away, apparently served a similar function.

Excavations at this hillfort were carried out in the 1990s by Zdenek Farkaš, and in 2018 to 2020 the Slovak National Museum conducted an archaeological excavation here under the direction of Pavol Jelínek, in which our civic association Hradiská took part as volunteers. During the excavation we discovered a great many very interesting finds, above all from the medieval period.

children.text: People of the Ludanice group (the Early Eneolithic) had already settled on Železník and in its surroundings, and later it was used in the Middle to Late Bronze Age, from which several metal finds come, and in the Hallstatt period. Its most pronounced occupation, however, was in the medieval period, roughly from the 11th to the 15th century, and there is good reason to suppose that in the 13th century it was the target of an attack by one of the armies of the day, most probably that of Přemysl Otakar II, to which we attribute the destruction of several fortlets in the Lesser Carpathians, for example the fortlet of Altenburg in Pezinok. The hillfort is of interest from an all-Slovak point of view in that around 2,000 counterfeit coins modelled on Viennese pfennigs, at various stages of production, were found on its summit and slopes. They were made from bronze vessels cut successively into long strips, from which square “blanks” were cut out; a faint square was then struck on them and finally they were silvered. More than 20 of these counterfeit coins were discovered during our excavation as well. The forger’s workshop was apparently located in the documented log building. The culprit was therefore apparently the local lord of the hillfort. Altogether some thousand objects were recorded here during the excavation in the 1990s, on the basis of which the whole process of forging money can be reconstructed – from the production of the coin blanks to their striking.

The finds of relatively numerous military items point to the possible military destruction of the hillfort at the end of the 13th century. During our excavation too we found, mainly on the south-western slope of the hillfort near the presumed gateway, a total of 6 iron arrowheads typical of the High Middle Ages and a total of 3 spurs, two of which can provisionally be dated to the 12th–13th centuries and one to the 15th century. The cross-guard from a falchion can also be assigned to this period. In addition, part of mail armour was found at the hillfort in the 1990s, which is a relatively rare find from the medieval period. During our excavation two very finely preserved Gothic keys were also discovered at the hillfort, along with buckles, knives, two fragments of medieval coins, a gombík, flower-shaped ornaments and other finds.

Another point of interest is the outwork with a deep ditch on the southern foot of the hillfort. Zdenek Farkaš states that the rampart was apparently never finished, and he supposes that it originated in the Bronze Age. We did not manage to find any finds in its immediate vicinity that might date it more closely.

children.text: This hillfort has a great genius loci and I recommend a visit to everyone. There is as yet no information panel on it, but I presume that our civic association Hradiská will create one in the future…
